title: Bridget of Sweden
hookLine: a widow, mother of a large family, founder, and visionary of the passion
last: IF YOU ARE WHAT YOU SHOULD BE.

lines: THE LIFE SHE BUILT IS OVER.
cards: What does a woman do when the life she built is suddenly over? In Sweden, a noblewoman has spent her married years running a household, raising a large family, serving at the royal court.
Tradition says she and her husband went on pilgrimage together, and not long after, he died. She is a widow now, her children growing up. She could step back into a quiet widowhood.
Instead, her work is about to begin. She will found a religious order, travel to Rome and never really come home, and write down visions that people still read.

teach.b: Bridget, or Birgitta in Swedish, didn't become a nun and disappear. She became something harder to describe. After her husband's death she gave herself to prayer, and visions came again and again.
Her early biographers say she had one even as a child; now they filled her life. They kept returning to the passion of Christ: his suffering on the cross, and his mother Mary standing near it.
They were gathered into books called her Revelations, full of the cross seen up close, painful and tender.

teach.h: AN ORDER, AND A HOUSE AT VADSTENA.
teach.b: She founded a religious order, often called the Bridgettines, with a great house at Vadstena in Sweden. Like Catherine, she wrote to the popes in Avignon and urged them back to Rome.

She went to Rome herself, lived there for years, and died there. One of her daughters, Catherine of Sweden, stayed with her and is honored as a saint too. The Bible pays particular attention to widows.

In Luke, when the infant Jesus is brought to the temple, an old widow named Anna is there, who, the King James Bible says, "departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day."
Widowhood, in that picture, isn't only loss; it can be a new kind of service.
James is just as blunt about everyone else's part: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction".
Catholics honor Bridget as a saint and a patron of Europe. Her life holds both a widow's grief and a widow's strength.

how: Catholics honor Bridget of Sweden as a saint and one of the patron saints of Europe, and Bridgettine sisters still live and pray in houses that trace back to her order.

o: a nun who nursed the sick of Rome through a plague
a Swedish widow who founded an order and saw visions
a queen of Sweden who brought the faith to the north

p: a great house of her order
the widow who served night and day

s: Bridget's Revelations and her order came after her husband died
as a widow she gave herself to prayer; the visions of her Revelations and her order followed.
Bridget stayed in Sweden all her life
she went to Rome, lived there for years, and died there.

games.q: you're a noblewoman in Sweden. your husband has died, and your children are growing up. what do you do with the rest of your life?
o: retire quietly to the family estate.
give yourself to prayer, found an order, and go to Rome.
games.why: Bridget's widowhood became the start of her work: visions, an order, letters to the popes, and Rome.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has lost a husband or a wife, a grandparent, a neighbor, a friend's mother, recently or long ago, and think about their days now: the meals, the empty side of the bed, the quiet evenings.
If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, hold them in your thoughts, with care.

wordCard.voice: Bridget. A widow and mother of Sweden who, after her husband's death, founded an order, saw visions of the passion, and spent her last years in Rome.

orig.note: Greek: widow, the word in James 1:27 and in Luke's story of Anna.
